planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Arusha coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container specimen brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Named for the Tanzanian town near Mount Meru where it has long been grown, Arusha is a tall, heirloom Typica-type Arabica distinguished from most other Typica lines by its unusually large leaves, bronze-tinted new growth, and oversized beans. Early coffee plantings on the volcanic slopes of the Eastern Highlands of Papua New Guinea during the colonial period drew on this same Tanzanian stock, so the variety has a long history in both regions even though it was never bred for high yield. Its vigorous, wide-spreading habit has made it as popular as a striking tropical foliage specimen as it has for its mild, sweet cup, but like other unimproved heirloom Typica types it carries little natural resistance to leaf rust or coffee berry disease. Give it deep, rich, well-drained acidic soil, dappled shade, and generous overhead room, since it grows noticeably larger and more sprawling than compact modern hybrid cultivars.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant seedlings into a warm, flooded paddy bed well after soil has warmed; Kilombero is a tall, photoperiod-sensitive traditional variety best suited to a long, humid, monsoon-like growing season.

directions: Kilombero takes its name from the broad floodplain of the Kilombero River in Tanzania's Morogoro Region, one of East Africa's most important rice-growing basins, where this tall traditional variety has long been favored over modern dwarf types for its distinctive aroma and soft, fluffy texture after cooking. Local millers and cooks rate it among the finest Tanzanian table rice, commanding a price premium over ordinary paddy rice in regional markets. Because it is a tall, lodging-prone landrace rather than a semi-dwarf modern cultivar, it performs best with standing water through most of the vegetative season and a sheltered bed rather than exposed, windy ground. Expect a long, warm growing season before harvest, similar to other traditional tropical lowland rice types.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) Tanzania rice value chain reports

planting.note: Plant disease-free stem cuttings (stakes) horizontally or at a slant, 2-4 inches deep, once soil has warmed well past 65°F; Kiroba is a long-standing favorite among smallholders in southern Tanzania for its reliable field performance.

directions: Kiroba is a cassava variety developed through Tanzania's national cassava breeding work centered at the Naliendele Agricultural Research Institute near Mtwara, and it has become one of the most widely grown varieties among smallholders in the coastal Mtwara and Lindi regions of southern Tanzania. It is valued for dependable root yields and reasonable tolerance of the cassava mosaic and brown streak pressures that devastate many older local landraces, without sacrificing the cooking quality farmers expect. Propagate from healthy stem cuttings planted horizontally in well-drained soil in full sun, and allow a full growing season of ten to fifteen months before the roots bulk to harvestable size. Like other cassava, it tolerates poor, sandy soils and periodic drought once established, making it a practical choice for marginal garden ground in warm climates.
sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) — Cassava in Africa country case studies

common_name: Karuka (Papua New Guinea Highland Pandanus Nut)

planting.note: Start from fresh seed, since viability drops quickly in storage; Karuka is native to cool, misty highland forest and tolerates cooler nights than most pandanus, but still needs frost-free conditions to establish.

directions: Karuka is a dioecious pandanus restricted to the cool mountain forests of the Papua New Guinea highlands, cultivated and semi-wild-harvested between roughly 1,800 and 2,800 meters elevation for the large, pineapple-shaped fruiting heads packed with oily, almond-flavored nuts that ripen during a distinct annual nut season. Because male and female trees are separate, growers need both sexes nearby for the female heads to fill out properly, and seedlings typically take the better part of a decade before their first bearing season. The nuts are a concentrated, prized source of fat and protein in a highland diet built mainly around starchy tubers, and whole fruiting heads are traditionally carried down to lowland markets and feasts. Grow in cool, humid, high-elevation conditions with rich, well-drained forest soil and filtered light, since lowland heat and intense sun are poorly tolerated.
sources: R.M. Bourke & T. Harwood (eds.), "Food and Agriculture in Papua New Guinea" (ANU Press)

common_name: Marita (Papua New Guinea Red Fruit Pandanus)

planting.note: Propagate from rooted basal suckers for faster, true-to-type establishment, or from fresh seed; plant in warm, humid, frost-free conditions in rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Marita produces massive, cylindrical, red-to-orange fruiting heads — sometimes over a meter long — whose oily pulp is simmered for hours into a rich, reddish sauce poured over sweet potato, taro, greens, and other starchy staples across the highlands and lowlands of Papua New Guinea. In a traditional diet built heavily around low-fat tubers, marita sauce is an important seasonal source of dietary fat and carotenoids, and its ripening is often marked by local feasts and trade between highland and lowland communities. The understory tree suckers readily from the base, so most growers propagate new plants from these basal shoots rather than waiting out the longer seed-to-fruit timeline. Give it warm, humid, sheltered conditions with consistently moist, fertile soil and filtered overhead light, and harvest fruiting heads once they have fully colored and the pulp has softened.
sources: R.M. Bourke & T. Harwood (eds.), "Food and Agriculture in Papua New Guinea" (ANU Press)

planting.note: Start from fresh seed in warm, humid conditions; okari is a large lowland tropical tree that needs many years of frost-free growth before it begins bearing.

directions: Okari is a towering lowland tree native to Papua New Guinea and found also in the Solomon Islands, grown for the large, hard-shelled nuts borne inside a fibrous fruit that are traditionally roasted over coals before cracking to reveal a rich, almond-like kernel. Mature trees bear heavily for decades once established, so a planting is as much an investment for future generations as it is a near-term food source, and village groves of large old okari trees are common across its range. The species demands deep, well-drained lowland tropical soil, full sun, and sustained warmth and humidity, with little tolerance for cool nights or any frost. Because seedlings need years of growth before their first nut harvest, most home gardeners outside the tropics will only encounter okari as a container foliage specimen rather than a bearing nut tree.
sources: R.M. Bourke & T. Harwood (eds.), "Food and Agriculture in Papua New Guinea" (ANU Press)

planting.note: Plant rooted suckers (followers) in deep, rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun once all frost danger has passed; Mchare bananas are shorter and more slender than East African Highland bananas and need less room between mats.

directions: Mchare is the collective name for a distinct group of diploid (AA genome) bananas grown almost exclusively on the fertile volcanic slopes around Mount Kilimanjaro in northern Tanzania, genetically separate from the triploid East African Highland bananas (matooke) that dominate banana growing elsewhere in the region. Kilimanjaro farmers maintain dozens of named local Mchare varieties distinguished by pseudostem color, bunch form, and use, with some favored for cooking while still starchy and green and others reserved for ripening as a sweet dessert fruit or fermenting into local banana beer. The group tends toward shorter, more slender plants with smaller bunches than highland AAA bananas, reflecting its separate introduction history into the region. Grow from rooted suckers in deep, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun, mulch heavily to conserve moisture, and thin each mat to two or three follower plants for steady, continuous bunch production.
sources: Bioversity International / INIBAP — East African AA banana genetic diversity studies
Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) banana genetic resources documentation
